Params: Some time before the Gray Raven Commandant falls into the sea...
<That was the first breath to fill your lungs. Before warmth, you knew cold. Before courage, you knew fear.>
These words... what do they... mean...
<You did not want to die. If you did not want to die, you must draw strength from other lives.>
<And so it became simple. A dagger pried open a shell. A harpoon pierced scales. Blood dispersed through the sea, so vivid and alive. Your flesh and your soul fed on your prey.>
<Then you realized the sea and the land are not so different after all.>
<You baited them with cooperation and prospects. Cut them with debt and calculation. Added a measured dose of violence, and those wrapped in costly garments became prey as well.>
<Endless wealth and power flowed from their wounds to you. They named you the beast of the sea, even after you had come ashore and pinned on that sun emblem. You wore the title with pride.>
What are... you... what... am I...
<You permitted no waste. This strength must serve to perfect life, as fuel to forge the new world.>
<But one day, you died. For no clear reason. For nothing.>
<Worse still, you did not die completely. You opened your eyes, and your prey was clinging to life upon your rotting corpse.>
<Insufferable! You thought, reaching out, only to find...>
The dreamlike veil over her mind scatters in an instant. Something cold presses against the side of her face—
Where did your body get blown to?
Arius Erhorn cradles her head in both hands and lets out a genuinely heartfelt sigh.
The remnant of a spine trails behind it, strung with charred cables and clotted blood. Arius pinches the half-heart still hanging from it and squeezes it.
The living can't fathom the regrets of the other shore, and the dead should never cling to life. You're neither. Compared to who you were back then, you're more like me now.
Inside the sealed chamber, the only glow comes from a pool of luminous blue water below.
The skull drops in, and impossibly, it makes no splash at all.
A moment later, a piercing shriek tears through the chamber.

Metal bones and sinew regrow in a rush. The pain of destruction reverses and floods her body, and yet it carries more than her own suffering. A chorus of voices from the dead of the Atlantic Eye erupts inside her skull.
In the water, the woman convulses, fingers raking at her own ribcage. She is trying to claw free the new flesh that torments her, but the regrowth outpaces her hands.
Don't make me watch—I don't want to listen—
She sees, in the crowded void of space, hostile aircraft hurl themselves at starships. Humanity destroys its own ark and never flies again.
She sees, in the crowded void of space, hostile aircraft hurl themselves at starships. Humanity destroys its own ark and never flies again.
She sees, beneath a great burning tree, the Red Tide sweep across the earth. The inhuman feed on the ruins of civilization and emerge transformed.
She sees, beneath a great burning tree, the Red Tide sweep across the earth. The inhuman feed on the ruins of civilization and emerge transformed.
Because this is the reality that already happened, hateful and pathetic as it is.
Maybe what's rebuilt with only half of the "Understanding" isn't quite perfect. Or maybe the kindling's material just can't hold up...
He descends the stairway of the Punishing Virus, each stride deliberate, until he reaches the pool. Then he leans down and presses her head beneath the water.
I will not permit waste. If your mind cannot hold steady, then let the dross be washed away, and you will become an extension of me.
The drowning woman slowly goes quiet. Arius touches the surface with one finger and begins talking to the ripples.
The other half of the Sefirah lies sunken in the deepest reaches of the Atlantic Eye. How laughable. As its creator, I find myself barred at the door.
Ananke... You must have schemed it for a very long time, Dominik... Its permissions have vanished from this world, together with your own existence.
To claim those permissions, I must go where you still exist, to the "time" in which you still live.
Did you truly believe I would walk in there and meet you myself, after all of this?
Many years ago, "Understanding" already unveiled the right answer to me—
All I need to do is push that Gray Raven Commandant—and Adelyde, led astray by your F.O.S.—back into your incomplete designs.
Beneath the water, a pair of jade eyes, tainted with crimson, tremble open.
Late at Night, Decades Ago. Sefirah Engine, Atlantic Eye.
...You dragged your partner to the bottom of the dam in the middle of the night, just to grill me about my disappointing student? You're not just trying to piss me off, are you, Mr. Erhorn?
Besides, that's the Helio family's own business.
The click of her heels rings through the vast chamber as she walks, her gaze climbing to the strange form of the Sefirah Engine. Her brow twitches.
(Where are the electric currents on those energy-transfer tentacles? I've never seen them quiet.)
Your own business? You drew no such boundaries when you asked me to help seize power from the current head of Helios, Rusalka.
That was part of our bargain. Surely you didn't walk away empty-handed.
From the moment you started the Purge, if I hadn't put our global heavy industry behind you and your pack of Kurono hyenas, what would you have had to take on Dominik in this tech race?
Backing me wasn't your choice. You had no choice.
Once Zero-point Energy works, it'll dump your entire energy sector in the trash. And space colonization will turn all your earthbound infrastructure into obsolete junk you can't haul with you.
The era takes off; you sink. You want a seat in the new order? You'd better hope I win.
Then give me something worth hoping for.
The Zero-point Reactor's about to hit its ignition test, so where is your progress?
This Sefirah you keep talking about, the one that can push human evolution past its limits, where is it?
Arius presses a key. Behind him, the sealed cubic structure unfolds layer by layer, ribbons of glowing blue light spreading outward like growing branches.
At the center of the chamber, a crystalline double helix turns in a slow, steady rotation, impossible to tell whether it is data or matter.
He extends both arms toward it, his grey-violet pupils drifting out of focus, his face near ecstatic.
This is my answer, my truth.
The energy swells and recedes around her like a tide, and Rusalka drifts toward the cube without meaning to.
Then the air splits with a whip crack. The cord coils around Arius and hauls him forward, cinched hard, until he stands before the tall woman.
Her longsword is out and at his neck in the same breath.
Give me a reason not to kill you right now and take the Sefirah.
Every one of you... so shortsighted, and so sure you've hidden it well.

With a single arm, he rips himself out of the whip's hold and closes his fingers around the edge of the sword. From where his palm touches the metal, tree-like veins flare to life, spreading swiftly up the blade toward the hand that holds it.
(Impossible! He's a cripple. How does his prosthetic even—)
What creator would hold back from touching their own creation?
(I can't move! Even my senses are being taken away!)
The moment the decryption finished, I linked myself in.
In that moment, I could understand all that can be perceived and define all that lies beyond perception.
The man, as if speaking only to himself, frowns and changes his tone.
Yet just before the gates of omniscience closed before me, I saw two figures standing beyond my reach, who harvested the fruit of my labor.
One had grey wings on their cloak, a stranger to me.
The other had your student's face.
Yes. Why her, indeed... Could it be that when Dominik selected her for the Watcher program all those years ago, he saw in her something I did not?
At that name, he scoffs and shakes his head.
As for the rest of you... predictable to the point of tedium.
A hunting beast always senses danger by instinct. You deliberately drove Adelyde away from the Atlantic Eye, did you not?
Arius takes Rusalka's stiff hand and presses it against the terminal she uses to give orders.
Her finger drops against her own will. In the silence of the deep, a communication chime sounds.
A Few Days Later, Far North Atlantic.

On an unfinished offshore platform, the night crew has just returned from below, gear stripped off, stomping their feet and rubbing their hands by the electric heaters while they wait for their bowls of hot soup.
A white-haired woman with red eyes steps out of the group. She lets down her long braid, flattened against her skull by the helmet, and takes two energy bars from the table.
She glances around for something and finds nothing. Confusion flickers, then fades into resignation.
Karin, where's my terminal? The survey data needs to get sorted and uploaded.
The girl she calls out to grins and waves the terminal in her hand.
It's my job today, Captain. You've been down three times. Call an energy bar dinner one more time and I'm chucking your terminal in the ocean!
From behind her back, she reveals what she has been holding: an opened metal can, fragrant steam curling from its mouth.
Just stole it from the kitchen. First can today! Drink it quick, before it goes cold.
She shoves the can into Adelyde's hand and guides her over to the heater with a firm hand. The crew has already arranged their mats into a loose ring, shifting closer to open a spot for her.
An older man with grey at his temples throws a blanket around her and flashes a toothy smile.
Would you look at our little lady captain! Face like stone, temper like iron, and tough all over. Peels off all that heavy dive gear and her hands don't even shake holding the soup.
As if long accustomed to this kind of teasing, Adelyde does not bother to look up, though she gives as good as she gets.
Shaky hands come from drinking too much when you were young.
Yeah, yeah, time for the old man to retire!
Hey, you ungrateful little brat! Captain shows up, teaches you a thing or two, and now you think you can talk back to me?!
Remember last time when you lost the sonar and I had to go down and haul it back up? Ring any bells?

Laughter and jeers rise in waves. The older man and the young woman are on the verge of a full-on squabble, so the workers hurriedly open a gap between them and, without missing a beat, plant themselves next to Adelyde.
Time really does fly... Can't believe the survey for this hellhole is almost finished.
Before you got here, everyone heard the same story. The heiress screwed up big, got kicked out, and they exiled her to our miserable, no-profit little site.
Not far off? The rumors were way uglier than that. We never expected you to tough it out like us, much less actually drag everyone through and crack the hard part.
And we holdouts can finally climb a little higher with this.
Her voice picks up an edge of frustration.
I never saw anything wrong with you. Whoever kicked you out was blind.
Exactly! If you ask me, they've got worse judgment than little Karin.
The girl's luck is unreal. She barely started, gets assigned to a project that's been stuck for years, and suddenly it's seeing daylight. Results come out and she's promoted just like that!
Adelyde takes a sip of her soup, smiles, and offers no defense.
You earned that promotion yourselves. Without your years of knowing these underwater currents, I wouldn't have known how to optimize the facilities effectively.
And you, Captain? Once the survey's done, where do you go?
Probably to the next project, same as always.
...Off to another place where nobody trusts you? Finish the job and walk away with nothing, not even your name on it?
The white-haired young woman looks down at the soup can in her hands, lifts it, and gives it a small shake.
If I wanted to, I could keep this can.
There'll always be people who believe in you, Captain.
The girl shoots to her feet, fists clenched.
I haven't told you yet, Captain, but I've made up my mind. I'm following you! No going back to land. Wherever you go, I go.
Only then does Adelyde frown. She sets the soup can aside, her expression turning serious.
Don't be reckless. Your future's not something to toss away. Think it through properly.
I'm not being reckless, I mean it! There's a lot I can learn with you—
Just then, the older worker lifts a hand, telling the girl to quiet down. He tilts his head as if listening for something, confusion creeping over his face.
You guys hear that? An aircraft, not cargo. Sounds military, and it's coming this way.
Military? It got past air defense... that means family clearance...
Stay here. I'll go take a look.
Something in her face closes off.

She rises and steps out into the wind, which lashes across the platform with sudden force. She raises her gaze against it, red eyes fixed, and watches a transport aircraft painted with the Helio emblem touch down.
The hatch opens. Two squads of soldiers in family colors pour out, fanning into a ring, rifles leveled at her.
The white-haired woman stands motionless, her expression giving nothing away.
Who sent you? What do you want?
The one at the front, fully masked, speaks through a voice distorter.
Direct orders from Lady Rusalka Helio: bring you back to the Atlantic Eye to see her.
Adelyde's eyes move across the armed figures around her.
Is this really necessary? What made you think I'd say no?
Her orders don't stop there. She wants you out of that garbage you're wearing and back into this.
The figure tosses a package toward her. Adelyde catches it and opens it.
Inside lies a neatly folded Helio family dress uniform, the same one she has refused to wear for years.
Put it on and come with us, or everyone peeking from back there eats bullets right alongside you.
Adelyde lifts her head, her gaze sharp. The leading soldier scoffs and raises the helmet's visor, revealing a face she knows.
A traitor to F.O.S. escorting a traitor to the Helios... Ironic, isn't it, Adelyde?
The young white-haired woman does not hesitate. Without a word, she walks back into the building under the escort of raised guns, pushes past her alarmed colleagues, and enters her room.
A moment later, the door opens again. Adelyde Helio steps out with her head high, once more draped in seafoam white and sapphire blue, and meets Alyssa's eyes.
I don't have anything to take. Let's go.
A small figure forces her way through the wall of armed soldiers and throws herself in front of Adelyde. Every gun swings toward her.
For the first time, Adelyde's expression changes. She pulls the girl behind her and shouts.
Who dares open fire on a family employee?!
She turns and takes Karin by the shoulders, her words quick but clear.
Listen, the data and the instrument calibration plan for the final phase are on the desk computer. No password.
Figure it out yourself. Keep at it and you'll learn. Everyone's relying on you.
Don't worry about me. The one calling me back is my teacher. She won't hurt me.
The young intern sniffles, her eyes rimmed red.
Can you take me with you?
Adelyde pats her arm in silence, gently releases her, and turns to walk away.
Her upright figure is soon swallowed by the wall of soldiers and disappears from view.
The flight is unnervingly quiet. Adelyde's movements are not restricted, but every seat around her is filled with masked soldiers gripping shock batons.
Behind her, ordinary engineers in TEC uniforms sit hunched over their terminals, pretending not to notice the unusual passenger or the tension in the cabin.
Through the porthole, the shapes of other transports emerge faintly from behind a low, heavy bank of dark clouds. Far in the distance below, the towering outline of the dam appears.
She watches in silence, lost in thought.
(This is a transport flight for engineers rotating back to the Atlantic Eye, not a detail sent just for me.)
(Either she wanted to keep this under wraps, or it was decided on the spot.)
(Why would Alyssa have my uniform? Was she the only one who set out separately?)
(Miss Rusalka... I haven't seen her in person since that competition. I wonder if she...)
She takes a slow breath and gathers herself. She has wrung every scrap of information from her surroundings, and whatever opening remains now lies with the people in this cabin.
She turns to Alyssa, who sits across from her in silence, and weighs her words before speaking.
You cut off everyone after graduation. Why did you—
She is only halfway through the sentence when a shock baton jabs into her shoulder and cuts her off.
She swallows the pant rising in her chest and allows herself no further reaction.
The weapon withdraws. Alyssa gives a sharp, contemptuous snort.
Behind the sweat-soaked bangs, the gaze that cuts toward her is still sharp.
That was unnecessary. You have a problem with me.
So what if I do? Your calm, self-righteous act makes me sick.
I'm not being righteous. I just don't want to get roughed up.
At those words, Alyssa's anger twists into a laugh.
That's exactly where I was back then. That teacher of yours handed me a gun. I had to either take it and secure a future, or turn it on myself.
Any idiot knew which way to go. What was I supposed to do against you TEC plutocrats?
I was even ready to be called a traitor, but I didn't expect—
Her teeth grind audibly, and her stare burns into Adelyde as though she means to bore straight through her.
You used me as a stepping stone to play hero and turned me into a joke.
Because of that speech, Arakna was judged too radical for the military, and I was cut from the line of succession. But you got what you wanted.
Her words land like a blow, stripped of any softness. She presses the baton into Adelyde's shoulder, forcing her flat against the backrest.

Your teacher is a fair employer, with reward and punishment in equal measure. She brought me into the Atlantic Eye, just as promised. Now even my family has been invited to Gardener Island for the Day of Enlightenment celebrations.
Once they see me drag you in to face punishment, they'll know that what everyone said back then meant nothing. That I chose right.
Adelyde's pupils contract sharply. At last, she realizes something is wrong.
Rusalka? The Day of Enlightenment celebration?
My teacher never celebrated the Day of Enlightenment. Who really gave you this order—
The blast exceeds anything the human ear can bear. Pain lances through her skull, and then there is no sound at all, not even the perception of it.
The dimensions of the world tear open. The great eye on the Atlantic snaps wide, glaring into the sky in torrents of glowing blue and blazing gold.
In myth, holy light descending from the sky signals divine revelation.
The pillar of light rising from the sea to pierce the heavens should have been humanity's crowning achievement in the Golden Age, the Helios' dream of a sun chariot ascending from the waves.
But the moment the shockwave sweeps through, colors dissolve, outlines drift, and a thousand sounds ring at once, unraveling the very concept of "Adelyde," layer by layer.
<color=#ffffffff><size=50>My/Our heart beats, unending. My/Our mouth holds gray, rotten ruin.</size></color>
My/our heart beats, unending. My/our mouth holds gray, rotten ruin.
<color=#ffffffff><size=50>I/We kneel to stone heaps through incense smoke. My/our gaze is cast beyond the galaxy.</size></color>
I/we kneel to stone heaps through incense smoke. My/our gaze is cast beyond the galaxy.
<color=#ffffffff><size=50>I/We suffer for each moment the world changes, and each moment it does not.</size></color>
<color=#ffffffff><size=50>I/We rejoice for each moment the world changes, and each moment it does not.</size></color>
I/we suffer for each moment the world changes, and each moment it does not. I/we rejoice for each moment the world changes, and each moment it does not.
She is an infant, a youth, an elder.
She is a hunter, a scientist, a farmer.
She speaks every language and carries every emotion.
She is everyone, and everyone is her.
Countless streams of golden light surge against the tide, and a pair of hands lifts a single drop of "water" from the "sea."
Adelyde snaps upright in her seat. Everyone around her has gone blank at the same instant, unresponsive to everything.
A heartbeat later, the aircraft lurches sharply, dragged upward by the column of surging luminous blue energy, and its frame groans in a way that bodes nothing good.
(Pilot's out cold, most likely. At this rate, we all die!)
She takes a deep breath and unclips the belt.
Her body drops, and she moves on pure instinct, weaving between seats and cabin walls, dodging bodies and obstacles, until she slams hard into the cockpit door.
Pain tears through her shoulder. The cramped space leaves her no room to reduce the impact.
She closes her eyes, grips the joint with her free hand, and shoves it back in with a hard, decisive push.
(Aww, can't lift my arm yet. Fine. Just one side...)
With her good arm, she catches a gun midair, grips it by the stock, and hammers it into the control panel.
One strike. Two. Three. The console dies under the blows.
She tucks her body and throws herself forward, a human ram, feet first, into the door.
The door gives. She surges through, pulls the unconscious pilot out of the chair, secures them behind the seat with a belt, and slides into the pilot's place.
Port Engine One and Starboard Engine Four are nominal. Engines Two and Three are overheating—
Reset power distribution and auto-select max total output. Flight parameter calibration set to manual. I'll do it.
Ahead of the cockpit windows, the energy surge deepens in color. Her fingers race across the instruments and the panel, then lock around the yoke and haul it hard against the pull.
Every ounce of strength is wrung from her body in the struggle against the surge and the steel. The agony is beyond measure now, but inside, her mind goes quiet.
Doing the impossible over and over, that's how you make it possible. All you need to do is...
Doing the impossible over and over, that's how you make it possible. All you need to do is...
The aircraft shudders and groans, and then the streams of light stretch, tear, and snap. With a sudden lurch, it breaks free of the surge.
Exhaustion floods through her all at once, pinning her to the seat, body and mind both drained.
Engine temperatures back within normal range. Returning to autopilot.
Alert! Armed individual detected in the cockpit!
The commotion behind her arrives muffled, like a sound heard from beneath the water.
Her fingers reach back, trembling. She turns her head, and cold metal presses against her throat.
She just saved all your lives.
I won't ask again. Drop it.
The muzzle pulls away from her neck, and Adelyde looks up.
A figure in a gray wing-patterned cloak stands in front of her, twin pistols aimed squarely at the family soldier's face.
She closes her eyes and laughs softly, her throat tight.
It's the words mouthed at their first parting.
It's the desperate cry of a child who wanted to meet again.
It's the last blessing she received before setting out for F.O.S.
